This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. A judge has ordered Tennessee officials
to preserve evidence related to the failed execution of Christa Pike last week. Today,
her attorneys said Pike is angry and confused, and she's aware of what happened. Catherine
Sweeney from member station WPLN reports.
She woke up after being unconscious for five days and being on a ventilator, but I'd say
there are two main takeaways after the court hearing in the press conference today. The
damage to her limbs and the damage to her brain. So, pentobarbital is alkaline. It's
like a drain cleaner and it causes burns and cellular damage. Her attorney said last week
she had burns and blisters on her arms, and today her arms and hands are severely swollen.
One of her attorneys said her hands look like an inflated surgical glove. The scope of her
brain damage is still being investigated, but here's her attorney, Randy Spivey.
I was not in the room when she woke up, so I don't want to speculate too much. Our understanding
was the first thing she said was, "Where am I and who are you?" There's still a lot of
cognitive confusion.
That report from WPLN's Catherine Sweeney. The Trump administration began sending $500
checks to some people with Obamacare plans. Ethics experts say the checks may violate
laws that prohibit government officials from using their office to influence elections,
as NPR's Selena Simmons-Duffin reports.
I spoke to Ellen Allen minutes after the check arrived at her house near Charleston, West
Virginia. I just can't believe it. I mean, that's crazy.
Ellen runs a small nonprofit called West Virginians for Affordable Healthcare. She has mixed feelings
about the money and the letter that came with it from the Trump administration.
I think it's more of a political stunt. If they cared really about the cost of healthcare,
they would do something that would make healthcare affordable for every American.
She says she plans to deposit the check in her health savings account and keep working
for healthcare for all. Selena Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
Tens of thousands of Israelis gathered in Tel Aviv today to mark the third anniversary
of the October 7th Hamas-led attack. The crowd included hundreds of grieving family members
and former hostages, as NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reports.
The event was at capacity, as a somber crowd watched tribute after tribute to commemorate
the deadliest day in Israel's history. It was organized by many of the bereaved family
members of those killed in the attack. The official state memorial was held on Monday.
The separate ceremonies reflect a deep divide between many Israelis and the government,
which has refused to establish a state inquiry into the failures that led to the disaster,
despite public pressure, to do so. Omri Shafroni, one of the family members of several killed
in the attack, called for accountability at the ceremony.
Not investigating the truth. We cannot fix things, he said. We cannot make sure it never
happens again.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reporting. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Maria Del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her Madrid home
sparked protests across Spain, has died. She became a symbol for renters struggling with
Spain's housing crisis. Despite a deal allowing her to return home, her health worsened. Her
case has galvanized a social movement, leading to a general strike in early elections called
by Spain's prime minister.
The World Wildlife Fund has published its biennial "Living Planet" report, which
chronicles a 73 percent drop in the average size of monitored wildlife populations from
1970 until 2022. Here's NPR's Ari Daniel.
This year's index adds almost 300 species, and the overall global decline in biodiversity
doesn't appear to be slowing down. But the report points to a handful of species that
have recovered or ticked upwards due to sustained conservation efforts — bluefin tuna, green
sea turtles, tigers, and certain populations of elephants. Rebecca Shaw is WWF's chief
scientist.
This gives us hints into how we should be doing conservation overall to reduce the systems
that drive the degradation of nature.
The report says, "collective hope is the most reliable predictor we have of whether
large-scale change will occur." Ari Daniel, NPR News.
The University of Nevada Las Vegas is set to graduate its first student with a minor
in mariachi. The program has launched to encourage students to become mariachi educators in the
local school district, where nearly 6,000 middle and high school students take part
in learning the popular Mexican folk music.
This is NPR News from Washington.
